extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors and educated literary readers (general 18th‑century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: General guidance and evaluative principles for writers on producing lasting literature and managing the work of writing and publishing (style, subject choice, practice, and dealing with critics/publishers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write on general principles for durability
rubrics_metrics.description: He that writes upon general principles, or delivers universal truths, may hope to be often read, because his work will be equally useful at all times and in every country; but he cannot expect it to be received with eagerness... He that lays his labours out upon temporary subjects, easily finds readers, and quickly loses them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer universal themes and principles if the goal is long‑term readership; topical or event‑driven works may gain rapid attention but will fade as circumstances change (example: Hudibras valued in its time for topical satire but largely forgotten later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules avoid faults but do not create beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules may obviate faults, but can never confer beauties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rules and prudential techniques to prevent obvious errors, but do not expect formal rules alone to produce originality or aesthetic excellence; risk and inventive departures from rules are often necessary to achieve extraordinary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive consultation can paralyse your work
rubrics_metrics.description: I read parts of my book to friends... None of them were satisfied; one disliked the disposition of the parts, another the colours of the style... I resolved to read no more, but to take my own way and write on, for by consultation I only perplexed my thoughts and retarded my work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early or excessive soliciting of diverse reader opinions can produce conflicting advice and stall progress; solicit feedback selectively and then follow your own judgement to complete the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field observation and empirical labour (genre‑specific requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural history is no work for one that loves his chair or his bed. Speculation may be pursued on a soft couch, but nature must be observed in the open air. I have collected materials with indefatigable pertinacity... Seven years I was employed in collecting animals and vegetables...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For observational or empirical genres (natural history, travel, reportage), rigorous fieldwork, direct observation, and extended time investment are required; armchair theorizing is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect publishing and patronage realities (practical preparedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: I expected the patrons of learning would contend for the honour of a dedication... I visited booksellers: some never dealt with authors; others had their hands full... One offered to print my work, if I could procure subscriptions for five hundred, and would allow me two hundred copies for my property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume automatic patronage or easy publication; be prepared for refusals, subscription models, or to self‑finance publication. Manage expectations about nobility, subscribers, and booksellers who may decline topical or voluminous works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and long time investment in material gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven years I was employed in collecting animals and vegetables, and then found that my design was yet imperfect... another year was to be spent in mines and coal-pits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High‑quality, substantive work often requires prolonged, patient collection and refinement of materials—plan for extended effort rather than expecting quick completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity and chance are crucial for wit and merriment
rubrics_metrics.description: Merriment is always the effect of a sudden impression. The jest which is expected is already destroyed... Nothing was ever said with uncommon felicity, but by the co‑operation of chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forced or overly rehearsed humour in performance writing or dialogue; cultivate conditions for spontaneous interaction and allow chance to generate the most felicitous comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism is easy and should be weighed against inventive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism is a study by which men grow important and formidable at a very small expense. The power of invention has been conferred by nature upon few...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that critics often exercise judgement at low cost compared to the labor of invention; do not be unduly discouraged by facile criticism—value constructive critique but recognise the asymmetry between criticizing and creating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fame is fickle; do not overvalue transient applause
rubrics_metrics.description: He that is loudly praised will be clamorously censured; he that rises hastily into fame will be in danger of sinking suddenly into oblivion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not orient creative practice primarily toward transient public applause; seek reasoned merit and durable qualities rather than short‑lived popularity, which may reverse quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in life (and art) prevents grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence... produces vigilance rather than elevation, rather prevents loss than procures advantage; and often escapes miscarriages, but seldom reaches either power or honour. It quenches that ardour of enterprise, by which every thing is done that can claim praise or admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cautious, overly prudent approach to one’s art may avoid failure but also stifle the boldness necessary for significant achievement; balance prudence with willingness to take creative risks.
